title: Grade 8 Science — Fri, May 30
description: Microorganisms — Day 5 of 5: Synthesis — friends vs foes, applications, and the bigger picture
subject: science

questions.question: A doctor tells a patient with a viral fever not to take antibiotics. Why?
options: Antibiotics are too expensive
Antibiotics only kill bacteria — they have no effect on viruses; overuse causes resistance
Antibiotics cure viral diseases faster
Antibiotics weaken the immune system needed to fight viruses
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial structures (cell wall, 70S ribosomes). Viruses don't have these structures — antibiotics are useless against viruses. Misuse creates antibiotic-resistant bacteria (superbugs) that threaten everyone.

questions.question: Herd immunity means:
options: Only cows and animals need vaccination
When enough people in a population are immune (vaccinated or recovered), disease cannot spread easily even to unvaccinated people
All members of a group must be sick at once
Immunity passed from mother to child only
questions.explanation: Herd immunity: when ~70-95% are immune (depending on disease), the pathogen can't find enough susceptible hosts to spread. Protects babies, immunocompromised people who can't be vaccinated. This is why high vaccination rates matter.

questions.question: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to:
options: Make medicines in laboratories
Clean up environmental pollution — oil spills, heavy metals, toxic waste — by breaking them down
Improve crop yield through genetic modification
Create new antibiotics from soil bacteria
questions.explanation: Bioremediation: microorganisms degrade or transform pollutants into harmless substances. Pseudomonas bacteria break down petroleum. Fungi remove heavy metals. Cheaper and eco-friendlier than chemical cleanup.

questions.question: Why is the human gut microbiome (trillions of bacteria in intestines) considered vital for health?
options: Gut bacteria cause all digestive diseases
Gut bacteria aid digestion, produce vitamins (K, B12), train the immune system, and protect against harmful pathogens
Gut bacteria are remnants of past infections
Gut bacteria only live in the large intestine and have no function
questions.explanation: Human microbiome: ~37 trillion microbial cells (roughly = human cells). They digest complex carbohydrates, produce vitamins, prevent colonisation by pathogens (competitive exclusion), and regulate immune response. Disruption (dysbiosis) linked to obesity, IBD, mental health.

questions.question: Why are viruses considered 'at the edge of life'?
options: They can live for billions of years
They have no cells, cannot carry out metabolism independently, and can only replicate inside a living host — yet they contain genetic material
They are found only in outer space
They were created artificially in laboratories
questions.explanation: Viruses: (1) Have genetic material (DNA or RNA). (2) Evolve. (3) Cannot reproduce independently — need host. (4) No metabolism, no cells, no organelles. They are the bridge between chemistry and life — debated by scientists.

questions.question: The 'germ theory of disease' (Pasteur, Koch) replaced which older idea?
options: Atomic theory of disease
Miasma theory — that disease was caused by 'bad air' from rotting matter
Genetic theory — diseases are inherited
Humoral theory — disease from imbalance of body fluids (Galen's idea)
questions.explanation: Before germ theory: miasma theory (bad smells/air cause disease) was dominant. Pasteur's experiments (swan-neck flask) proved microorganisms cause contamination. Koch identified specific bacteria for TB (1882) and cholera (1883). This transformed medicine.

questions.question: CRISPR-Cas9 uses a bacterial defence mechanism to:
options: Kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Edit DNA precisely in any organism — cutting and replacing specific gene sequences
Produce vaccines rapidly
Detect viruses in blood samples
questions.explanation: CRISPR = Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. Bacteria use it to 'remember' viruses. Scientists repurposed it as a 'molecular scissors' to edit genes. Used in disease research, treating genetic disorders, crop improvement.

questions.question: Emerging infectious diseases (EIDs) like COVID-19, Ebola, and SARS arise mainly because:
options: Scientists create them in laboratories
Pathogens mutate and jump from animal hosts to humans (zoonotic spillover), often due to deforestation and human-wildlife contact
All new diseases come from water contamination
They are genetic mutations in humans
questions.explanation: Most EIDs are zoonotic (from animals): HIV (chimpanzees), Ebola (bats?), SARS-CoV-2 (bats/pangolins). Deforestation, wildlife trade, and climate change increase human-animal contact, creating spillover opportunities.

questions.question: If food is sealed in cans, why can botulism still occur?
options: Canning does not kill any bacteria
Clostridium botulinum grows anaerobically inside sealed cans (no oxygen) and produces the deadly botulinum toxin
The can metal reacts with food to create the toxin
Botulism comes from the outside air, not the food
questions.explanation: C. botulinum thrives in anaerobic (no oxygen) conditions. A sealed can is perfect! The bacteria produce botulinum toxin — the most potent biological toxin known (LD50 ~1.3 ng/kg). Proper canning requires 121°C steam sterilisation to kill spores.

questions.question: Why do organisms that live in the deep ocean's hydrothermal vents not need sunlight?
options: They capture moonlight through bioluminescence
They use chemosynthesis — bacteria oxidise chemicals like hydrogen sulphide for energy instead of sunlight
They have evolved eyes that can see tiny amounts of light
They stored energy from surface photosynthesis and migrated down
questions.explanation: Chemosynthetic bacteria at hydrothermal vents: use H₂S + O₂ → SO₄²⁻ + energy. These bacteria support entire ecosystems (tube worms, crabs) without sunlight. This discovery changed our understanding of what conditions can support life.

questions.question: Which scenario represents beneficial use of a harmful microorganism concept?
options: Using Clostridium botulinum toxin (Botox) for medical/cosmetic muscle relaxation
Allowing E. coli to contaminate drinking water
Using Plasmodium to develop malaria treatments
Releasing Vibrio cholerae into rivers to study disease spread
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin = deadly, but in tiny purified doses → Botox (cosmetic wrinkle treatment) and medical treatment for muscle spasms, migraines. Many poisons have medical uses in controlled doses. Venom → antivenom, digitalis from foxglove → heart medicine.

questions.question: The chain of infection requires: pathogen + reservoir + mode of transmission + susceptible host. Breaking which link is vaccination targeting?
options: The mode of transmission
The reservoir
The susceptible host — making them immune so they cannot become infected
The pathogen directly
questions.explanation: Vaccination targets the susceptible host — it makes them immune so even if exposed to the pathogen via any route, they don't get infected. Other interventions: quarantine (reservoir), handwashing (transmission), antibiotics (pathogen).

questions.question: Why is it important to complete the full course of antibiotics even after feeling better?
options: To prevent constipation from antibiotic use
Stopping early leaves surviving bacteria (the resistant ones) to multiply and cause a relapse with drug-resistant infection
Antibiotics must be taken for exactly 10 days always
Antibiotics continue working for weeks after the last dose
questions.explanation: When you feel better, most bacteria are dead — but some resistant ones may survive. Stopping early gives them a chance to multiply. The surviving bacteria are more resistant than the original population → harder-to-treat relapse. Always complete the course.

questions.question: Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that only infect bacteria. How could they be used medically?
options: As antibiotics that also work against viruses
As 'phage therapy' to specifically kill targeted bacteria including antibiotic-resistant strains, without harming human cells
To create new vaccines against viral diseases
To kill cancer cells in the body
questions.explanation: Phage therapy: phages infect and kill specific bacteria. Since phages are highly specific (each phage targets one bacterial strain), they could kill superbugs without disturbing good gut bacteria. Research ongoing — may be key to post-antibiotic era.

questions.question: Week synthesis — classify as FRIEND or FOE: Yeast in bread / Plasmodium / Rhizobium / Influenza virus / Lactobacillus
options: Friend / Foe / Friend / Foe / Friend
Foe / Foe / Friend / Friend / Friend
Friend / Friend / Foe / Foe / Friend
Friend / Foe / Foe / Foe / Foe
questions.explanation: Yeast (FRIEND: makes bread). Plasmodium (FOE: malaria). Rhizobium (FRIEND: nitrogen fixation). Influenza virus (FOE: flu). Lactobacillus (FRIEND: curd, gut health). Summary: microorganisms are both friends and foes — context determines which!
